meta.about: Lemon Tree Hotels Ltd is largest mid-priced and the third largest overall hotel chain in India. It operate in the upscale segment and in the mid-priced sector, consisting of the upper-midscale, midscale and economy segments. It delivers differentiated yet superior service offerings, with a value-for-money proposition.[1]

scheme.steps: Step 1: Carnation Hotels and Hamstede Living merge into Lemon Tree. Part A: four 100% subsidiaries (Oriole Dr. Fresh, Sukhsagar Complexes, Manakin Resorts, Canary Hotels; 4 hotels, 359 rooms) merge into Fleur for 0.58 cr Fleur shares to Lemon Tree. Part B: 11 operating hotels (1,204 rooms), Aurika Shimla, the Shillong investment and the development team are demerged into Fleur; Lemon Tree shareholders get 20 Fleur shares for every 311 Lemon Tree shares (5.09 cr Fleur shares). Fleur then lists.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Lemon Tree Hotels Ltd (consolidated, Rs crore). One reported segment (hotels); we forecast it in two streams (owned and leased hotels; fees from third-party managed and franchised hotels; businessLines.hotel, checked against the segment in LEMONTREE.ctx.js). Operating EBITDA is post-Ind AS 116 and excludes other income. Minorities (41.09% of Fleur Hotels, Warburg Pincus) have no engine line: they sit in the tax rate (see _taxWhy) and in the SOTP. We model the group as it stands on 30-Sep-2026 (the Fleur scheme is not yet effective); the scheme is a sensitivity.

segments.name: Hotels (owned, leased and managed)
segments._why: Sum of the two streams in businessLines.hotel. Owned and leased hotels +8% / +10% / +9%: Q1FY27 owned revenue +7% (RevPAR +6%: occupancy +314 bps, ARR +2% as the West Asia shock pushed the mix to retail); 'July was great ... August solid', double-digit growth from Q2 guided (10-Aug-2026 call); Keys RevPAR +19% after renovation; Aurika Shimla (90 rooms) opens in FY27, Aurika Shillong (165, leased) in H2FY28, Varanasi (47) in FY29; ICRA (29-Sep-2026) sees premium-hotel revenue +7-9% in FY27. Third-party fees +30% / +28% / +30%: FY26 +23%, Q1FY27 +42%; ~2,000 keys to open in FY27 and ~5,000 rooms signed in FY26 open around FY29.
segments._marginWhy: Operating EBITDA margin FY24 48.8%, FY25 49.3%, FY26 47.8% (renovation, technology and the GST change cost 5.8% of revenue), Q1FY27 43.4% vs 44.5% (GST input-credit loss 2.3% of revenue, SAR provision 0.8%). Guide: FY27 net margin 'well better than' 47%, FY28 at least 50% as renovation and GST costs fall to ~3.7% of revenue. 47.8% / 49.5% / 50.5%: FY27 flat on FY26 (GST full year offsets lower renovation), then the guided step-up, rising fee mix in FY29; we stay a little below the 50% FY28 guide on an operating basis (the company figure includes ~0.5 pp of other income).

assumptions._unallocLabel: Corporate costs not in the segment
assumptions._unallocWhy: Single reported segment: the segment is consolidated operating EBITDA.

businessLines._why: FY26 base: revenue from operations Rs1,444.5 cr = fees from third-party managed and franchised hotels Rs73.9 cr (Q4FY26 call) + owned and leased hotels Rs1,370.6 cr (remainder). Fees from Fleur (Rs95.8 cr) are intra-group. Growth per stream in segments[0]._why.

assumptions._capexWhy: CRISIL (17-Jul-2026): capex of Rs90-100 cr a year over FY27-29 to add about 250 premium keys (Aurika Shimla, Shillong, Varanasi) plus renovation capex, funded from accruals and debt; renovation spend to fall towards ~1% of revenue from FY28 (10-Aug-2026 call). Aurika Nehru Place (572 rooms; capex 'to be announced', opening FY30 or later) and Warburg-funded acquisitions (~2,500 keys under discussion, none signed) are not in our numbers.
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation Rs139 cr (assets Rs113 cr + right-of-use Rs25 cr) = 3.0% of the model gross block (Rs4,693 cr incl. right-of-use); Q1FY27 Rs36 cr (Rs145 cr annualised). 3.1% gives ~Rs148 cr in FY27E, rising with capex.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: Zero: Lemon Tree has net debt; finance income is built in otherIncome.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener basis (other income + finance income + share of associates, before exceptional items): FY26 Rs8.2 cr + Rs12.3 cr − Rs0.9 cr = Rs19.6 cr; Q1FY27 Rs2.1 cr + Rs4.1 cr − Rs0.3 cr = Rs5.9 cr (Rs24 cr annualised, includes interest on ~Rs200 cr of cash). Rs20 / 22 / 24 cr: interest on cash, miscellaneous income; no exceptional items.
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 Rs179.5 cr (borrowings Rs136.7 cr + leases Rs42.8 cr); Q1FY27 Rs40.5 cr (Rs29.8 cr + Rs10.7 cr) on gross debt of Rs1,475 cr at 7.48%, falling each quarter (Rs1,658 cr a year earlier). We let free cash flow (~Rs370-540 cr a year in our model) repay bank debt, as the company has done since FY24 (CRISIL: Rs180-200 cr of scheduled repayments a year; aim to be debt-free at Lemon Tree in 3-4 years): bank interest ~Rs105 / 75 / 45 cr at ~7.4% plus lease interest ~Rs43-46 cr (Shillong from FY28). Acquisitions with Warburg money would add debt and EBITDA; neither is in our numbers.
assumptions._taxWhy: Tax plus minorities (engine workaround: no minority line). FY25: attributable Rs197 cr on PBT Rs296 cr = 33.5% leakage; FY26 before exceptional items: Rs245 cr on Rs392 cr = 37.6%; Q1FY27: tax Rs21.8 cr + minorities Rs11.3 cr on PBT Rs79.1 cr = 41.8%. 41%: tax ~25.5% of PBT (Q1 27.6%; FY26 19.7% helped by deferred tax) plus minorities ~21% of profit after tax (FY26 21.2%, Q1 19.7%; Warburg's 41.09% of Fleur).
assumptions._payoutWhy: No dividend for FY26 (AR FY26) or any earlier year; cash goes to debt reduction and, after the scheme, to Fleur's growth.

dcf._betaWhy: The engine discounts at the cost of equity; Lemon Tree carries debt, so beta 0.8 sets the rate at 11.3%, our WACC: cost of equity ~12.5% (beta 1.0) on ~83% of capital, post-tax debt ~5.6% (7.48% × 0.75) on ~17% (net debt incl. leases ~Rs1,800 cr vs ~Rs8,700 cr market value).
dcf._tgWhy: Indian travel grows with nominal GDP; 6% nominal, as for the other hotel reports.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~10% to 8% by year 15 as fee growth normalises.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: 52%: a rising share of fees (75-80% margin business) on a mid-market owned base that earns ~45-50%.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex fades to 6% of revenue: Lemon Tree (asset-light) needs little; the owned base needs renovation (~2-3%) and some growth keys.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Corporate travel recovers fast after the West Asia shock, ARR grows ~8-10% a year, Keys and the renovated hotels re-price, managed openings run ahead of the 2,000-key FY27 target, margins pass 50% in FY28 and the market pays the top quartile of Lemon Tree's own post-Covid multiple after the same sector move.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Corporate demand stays soft, new supply weighs on Mumbai and Gurugram, ARR stalls, GST and renovation costs fall more slowly, managed openings slip and the multiple stays at the bottom quartile after the sector de-rating.

cover.headline: India's mid-market hotel leader at ~30% below its post-Covid multiple; the margin promise and the Fleur split are the triggers, the debt and the minorities are the catch
cover.lead: Lemon Tree runs 135 hotels (11,946 rooms) under Aurika, Lemon Tree, Red Fox and Keys; it owns or leases 5,759 rooms (mostly through Fleur Hotels, 41.09% owned by Warburg Pincus) and manages 6,187 for others, with 11,435 more signed. Q1FY27 revenue rose 9% but room rates only 2% (the West Asia shock hit corporate travel) and the operating margin fell to 43.4% (GST, stock-appreciation rights). The street values the stock on **EV/EBITDA on FY28E**, adjusted for the Fleur minority (six Buys, median target ₹142). Lemon Tree trades at 14.2x one-year-forward EV/EBITDA against a post-Covid median of 20.1x; its three usable listed peers (IHCL −17%, EIH −26%, ITC Hotels −20%) had de-rated by a median −20% by 30-Sep-2026. The house rule gives **16x Sep-28E EBITDA**; less minorities (21% of equity value) and net debt, the sum of the parts is **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY.** We forecast EBITDA of ₹753 / 867 / 977 cr and EPS of ₹3.6 / 4.6 / 5.7 (FY27-29E). Cross-checks are higher (P/E ₹159, DCF ₹167). Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The leader of a supply-short segment
arguments.p: Owned hotels ran at 73.5% occupancy in FY26 with ARR of ₹6,875 (+8%), the best year in the company's history; 6,187 managed rooms and a 11,435-room signed pipeline make it the largest mid-market platform in India. Third-party fees grew 42% in Q1FY27.

arguments.h: Margins should recover as renovation ends
arguments.p: Renovation, technology and the GST change cost 5.8% of revenue in FY26; management guides ~3.7% from FY28 and a margin of at least 50% (operating 47.8% in FY26, 43.4% in Q1FY27). We model {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} and EPS growth of ~22% a year (FY26-29E, before one-offs) as interest falls.

arguments.h: But debt, minorities and a complex split
arguments.p: Net debt incl. leases was ₹1,833 cr at Mar-26 (2.6x EBITDA); Warburg Pincus owns 41.09% of Fleur, and minorities took 21.2% of FY26 profit after tax. The scheme that makes Lemon Tree asset-light and lists Fleur still needs SEBI, NCLT and shareholder approval (management: CY2027), and Fleur plans to spend ₹2,500-3,000 cr on growth.

arguments.h: Valuation: the stock fell further than the sector
arguments.p: At ₹104 the market pays ~12.1x Sep-28E EBITDA on our numbers; our derived multiple is 16x. Lemon Tree's own trailing EV/EBITDA sits 39% below its median, against 20% for the peers. The DCF needs a ~13.8% discount rate to justify the price, above our 11.3%. The rule stays BUY below ~₹120.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management called July "great" and August "solid" and expects double-digit growth from Q2, with ARR back as the driver.
The scheme: SEBI and stock-exchange observations, then the NCLT filing and shareholder and creditor meetings; Fleur listing in CY2027 on management's estimate.
Warburg Pincus's up to ₹960 cr primary investment in Fleur and the "bunch of announcements" on acquisitions management expects within ~6 months of 10-Aug-2026.
Peak season (Oct-Mar): corporate travel after the West Asia shock, 40+ wedding dates and the MICE calendar; ARR above ₹7,500 cuts the GST cost.
Openings: Aurika Shimla (90 rooms, FY27), ~2,000 managed keys targeted in FY27, Aurika Shillong (H2FY28).

sections.title: A mid-market hotel owner that is turning itself into a hotel manager: 5,759 owned rooms, 6,187 managed, 11,435 signed

blocks.p: Lemon Tree makes money in two ways. **Owned and leased hotels** (41 hotels, 5,759 rooms at Jun-2026, 7 of them leased) keep all their revenue and costs; they produced ~95% of FY26 revenue (₹1,371 cr of ₹1,445 cr). Most of these hotels, including Aurika Mumbai Skycity, sit in **Fleur Hotels**, a subsidiary that Lemon Tree owns 58.91% of; Warburg Pincus bought the other 41.09% from APG in May-2026. **Managed and franchised hotels** (94 hotels, 6,187 rooms) belong to other owners, who pay Lemon Tree fees for the brand, distribution, loyalty programme and management: ₹73.9 cr in FY26 (+23%) and ₹22.8 cr in Q1FY27 (+42%). Fleur also pays Lemon Tree fees (₹95.8 cr in FY26), but these cancel out in the consolidated accounts.

The brands span the middle of the market: Aurika (upscale; Udaipur and Mumbai), Lemon Tree Premier (upper midscale), Lemon Tree Hotels (midscale), Red Fox (economy) and Keys (Prima, Select, Lite), in 80+ cities, plus Dubai, Bhutan and Nepal. Owned-hotel occupancy was 73.5% in FY26 and ARR ₹6,875, both records. The company reports one segment, so the profit split between owned hotels and fees is visible only in the pro-forma accounts of the planned split (Lemon Tree: FY26 revenue ₹247 cr, EBITDA ₹149 cr; Fleur: ₹1,333 cr and ₹554 cr).

blocks.callout: **Why the model matters:** a mid-market hotel is cheap to build and run (no ballrooms, few restaurants), so Lemon Tree's owned hotels earn hotel-level EBITDAR margins of ~45-60% (52% for all owned hotels in Q1FY27) at daily rates of only ₹4,100-9,200. But owning means debt and slow growth. The fee business needs almost no capital and should earn 75-80% margins at scale, which is why the company wants to separate the two: Lemon Tree as the manager, Fleur as the owner.

sections.title: Demand still ahead of supply, but FY27 slowed: the West Asia shock hit corporate travel and the GST change hit mid-market rooms

blocks.p: Indian hotel demand has outgrown branded supply for four years, and Lemon Tree argues the mid-market, especially in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, is where branded supply is thinnest; its own hotels run at 73-79% occupancy. ICRA (29-Sep-26) expects premium-hotel revenue to grow 7-9% in FY27 after 11% in FY26, with occupancy 72-74%. Two things went against Lemon Tree's segment in 2026. First, the West Asia conflict cut inbound travel and, "as a second-order effect", corporate trips: large companies told their managers to use video calls. Second, the GST change: rooms sold below ₹7,500 a night lost input-tax credit, which cost Lemon Tree 2.3% of revenue in Q1FY27. The Executive Chairman argues the cycle has not peaked: India's occupancy is "still mid-60s", while an up-cycle starts at 70-72%.

blocks.p: Lemon Tree charges hotel owners fees for its brands, reservations, loyalty programme (2.5 m members; 45% of demand is repeat) and management. Signings have run ahead of openings for three years (~2,000 rooms, then ~3,500, then 4,912 in FY26), and hotels open ~30-36 months after signing, so management expects openings of ~2,000 keys in FY27 and ~5,000 around FY29. blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Lemon Tree has a real cost and distribution advantage in a fragmented segment, and its brands are what owners sign for. That is a moat in the fee business. In the owned hotels there is no pricing moat: Q1FY27 showed that when corporate demand weakens, rates give way. The value of the franchise will show up in fee growth, not in rates.

sections.title: Revenue 2.2x pre-Covid and margins up from ~36% to ~48%; but margins have slipped for two years and a fifth of the profit goes to minorities

blocks.p: Consolidated revenue was ₹669 cr in FY20, fell to ₹252 cr in FY21 (Covid) and reached ₹1,444 cr in FY26. The rebound was fast (FY23 ₹875 cr, +118%; FY24 ₹1,071 cr, +22%; FY25 ₹1,286 cr, +20%) as Aurika Mumbai Skycity opened in Oct-2023 and room rates rose. FY26 grew 12%. Operating EBITDA margin jumped from 36% in FY20 to 51% in FY23, then eased to 49% in FY24-25 and **47.8% in FY26**, because Lemon Tree expensed a large renovation programme, invested in technology and lost GST input credit on rooms below ₹7,500 (together 5.8% of revenue in FY26). Profit attributable to shareholders was ₹197 cr in FY25 and ₹227 cr in FY26 (₹245 cr before the labour-code charge); minorities (Fleur Hotels' outside shareholder) took another ₹61 cr.

sections.title: Earnings quality: real cash and conservative renovation accounting, but a fifth of the profit is the minority's and debt is still high

bullets: **Renovation is expensed.** Renovation is mostly expensed (opex), not capitalised: renovation + technology + GST impact was 5.8% of revenue in FY26 (renovation ~4.2%, technology ~0.6%, GST ~1.0% for half a year; Q1FY27 deck slide 21), which depresses reported margins while the programme runs. That flatters nothing: it depresses today's margin and should reverse.
**Definitions.** The company's 'net EBITDA' includes other income (FY26 Rs8.2 cr); Screener operating EBITDA excludes it (Rs690 cr). We use operating EBITDA throughout, as Screener and the peers do.

**Exceptional items.** FY26 exceptional charge Rs33.3 cr (new labour codes, Q3FY26) and Rs1.9 cr in Q4; Screener after-tax Rs23 cr. FY26 attributable profit ₹227 cr reported, ₹245 cr before the exceptional charge (Screener "Profit for PE").

**Minorities.** Large: ₹61.2 cr in FY26 (21.2% of profit after tax; 19.3% in FY25), ₹11.3 cr in Q1FY27. Warburg Pincus (Coastal Cedar Investments B.V.) 41.09% of Fleur Hotels since 22-May-2026; APG before.
**Stock appreciation rights.** Stock appreciation rights (cash-settled): provision Rs2.6 cr in Q1FY27, marked to the share price.
**Cash conversion.** Operating cash 79% of operating EBITDA in FY26 (85% in FY25); free cash flow ₹406 cr went to debt repayment.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The cash is real and the renovation accounting is conservative. But headline "EBITDA" and "PAT" are before a minority that takes ~21% of profit, the company's EBITDA includes other income, the GST and SAR adjustments in the "adjusted" figures are recurring costs, not one-offs, and the scheme will soon make the consolidated history hard to compare.

sections.title: Debt is falling but still heavy: ₹1,500 cr of bank debt plus ₹503 cr of leases, 2.6x EBITDA; minorities own a third of the equity

blocks.p: Unlike IHCL, EIH and ITC Hotels, which hold net cash, Lemon Tree is a borrower. At Mar-2026 it owed ₹1,500 cr to banks (₹1,699 cr a year earlier) and ₹503 cr of lease liabilities, against ₹171 cr of cash, bank balances and investments, so **net debt including leases was ₹1,833 cr** on Screener's figures (2.6x FY26 operating EBITDA; CRISIL 2.63x). Bank debt fell to ₹1,475 cr at Jun-2026 at a 7.48% cost. The equity side is unusual: of ₹2,079 cr of total equity, **₹687 cr (33%) belongs to minorities**, mostly the 41.09% of Fleur Hotels that APG sold to Warburg Pincus on 22-May-2026. CRISIL rates the bank lines A+ on "Watch Developing" until the scheme is approved; ICRA reviewed its rating in Aug-2026. After the scheme, all the group's debt moves to Fleur and Lemon Tree becomes debt-free.

blocks.p: Six standing views dated on or before 30-Sep-2026, all Buy. Four updated after Q1FY27 (10-11 Aug-2026); IDBI Capital and Keynote last published in Jun-2026 (after Q4FY26). Methods: EV/EBITDA on FY28E, with the Fleur minority taken out either by deducting APG's/Warburg's share of Fleur EBITDA or by a SOTP of the fee business and the owned business. The median of the six targets is **₹142**, 36% above the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹104. The disclosed methods differ in how they treat Fleur: ICICI Direct puts 20x on consolidated FY28E EBITDA after removing APG's 41.09% of Fleur's EBITDA (but deducts all the group's debt); Motilal Oswal puts 17x on standalone EBITDA and Lemon Tree's share of Fleur and 30x on the management company; PL puts 22x on the fee business and 20x on the owned business. On our numbers the median target implies ~16.1x Sep-28E EBITDA. Targets were higher in January 2026 around the scheme announcement (ICICI Direct Rs185 on 24x FY27E with a 25% holdco discount; Motilal Oswal Rs200); they were cut through 2026 as the stock fell from ~Rs180 to ~Rs105 with the West Asia shock and the GST change.

sections.title: Valuation: 16x Sep-28E EBITDA, less minorities and net debt, gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}; the stock has de-rated twice as far as the sector

blocks.h: How the street values Lemon Tree

blocks.p: Hotel companies in India are valued on **EV/EBITDA** (enterprise value ÷ operating profit before depreciation): every broker that disclosed a method for Lemon Tree uses FY28E EBITDA, with the Fleur minority taken out, and the published IHCL, EIH and ITC Hotels reports use the same yardstick. We use Sep-28E EBITDA (½ FY28E + ½ FY29E, the 12-month-forward year the market will look at in September 2027) in a sum of the parts: 100% of consolidated EBITDA at the derived multiple, less the minorities' share of the resulting equity value, less net debt including leases.

The hotels and the management business are valued on 100% of Sep-28E operating EBITDA (₹922 cr), with lease liabilities in net debt. Minorities (almost all Warburg Pincus's 41.09% of Fleur) took 21.2% of FY26 profit after tax (19.3% in FY25, 19.7% in Q1FY27), so we deduct 21% of the equity value (hotel EV less net debt): ₹37 a share. This is the same gross-up we apply to the price history, so the multiple and the deduction are consistent. Net debt is the model's Sep-28E figure: free cash flow repays bank debt in our forecasts, and we add nothing for Warburg's capital or Fleur's acquisitions. The scheme, if approved on its terms, would add ~₹8 a share (Fleur split chapter).

blocks.p: House rule: start from the stock's own one-year-forward EV/EBITDA, adjust for how far the sector had moved against its own history by 30-Sep-2026, then test growth, peers, returns and the street. (1) **Window.** Lemon Tree's EBITDA broke from the Covid trough (FY21 ₹57 cr, FY22 ₹119 cr) to ₹448 cr in FY23; on realised forward EBITDA the 2021-22 multiples look artificially low, because the market could not see the rebound, so the turnaround rule starts the window at the break (1-Apr-2022), as for IHCL and EIH, and measures the peers' move over the same window; the since-2021 median is a sensitivity. (2) **EV includes minorities**, because the SOTP values 100% of EBITDA and then deducts them (gross-up ~18-21%); without it the median is 17.2x. (3) **Peers.** Three usable peers (IHCL, EIH, ITC Hotels), the minimum, so the set is not widened: Chalet is out (residential flat sales in its trailing EBITDA) and ITC Hotels is measured over the window it has (since 1-Apr-25, listing months skipped). Subsets are sensitivity rows.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good mid-market franchise priced for the 2026 shock; buy it for the margin recovery and the fee growth, not for the rates

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest mid-market hotel platform, owned hotels at ~74-76% occupancy and ~52% hotel-level margins, a fee business growing 23-42% a year with a signed pipeline almost twice today's managed rooms, and a plan to separate the asset-light manager from the asset owner with Warburg Pincus's capital. Attributable EPS should grow ~22% a year as margins recover and debt falls.

**What you are paying:** 14.2x one-year-forward EV/EBITDA (its own post-Covid median is 20.1x) and 22.6x our FY28E EPS. The peers sit ~20% below their medians; Lemon Tree 39% below its own. On the street's method with our inputs and the house rule for the multiple, the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a BUY. The rating does not need a re-rating of the sector, only that Lemon Tree trades in line with it. Without the sector adjustment the same SOTP gives ~₹175.
